Title: How to Add an Outlet to a Finished Wall the Right Way (No Patching, No Mess)
Reference: "How To Add An Outlet To A Finished Wall" · 13,297,508 (Everyday Home Repairs, 2022-06-16) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nWfEANZOYSk
Brief: Adding a receptacle to a finished wall without attic, basement or crawl-space access means taking power from an existing receptacle on the same wall and running cable sideways behind the baseboard, where the trim hides every drywall cut. Needed: trim puller, oscillating multi-tool, stud finder, extension drill bit, fish tape, voltage tester, NM cable the same size as the existing wire (14 AWG on a 15 A breaker, 12 AWG on a 20 A breaker), a cable connector, an old-work box, listed connectors and a tamper-resistant receptacle. Steps: 1) pull the baseboard and snip its nails from the back; 2) cut a drywall strip, only drywall-deep, low enough for the trim to cover it; 3) turn off the breaker and verify dead with a tester before opening the existing box; 4) drill through each stud, keeping the hole edge 1-1/4 in. from the stud face or adding a steel nail plate (NEC 300.4(A)(1)), since trim nails go into those studs; 5) fish the cable; NM entering a metal box needs a clamp or connector, with the sheath at least 1/4 in. inside (NEC 314.17); 6) leave 6 in. of free conductor, 3 in. past the box face (NEC 300.14); 7) check box fill: 2.00 cu in. per 14 AWG, 2.25 per 12 AWG, double for the receptacle, all grounds counted once (NEC 314.16); 8) pigtail the old receptacle and the new run together. Kitchen countertop circuits may serve only kitchen, pantry and dining areas, bathroom receptacle circuits only bathrooms, and a new outlet adds load to a circuit already in use. Extending a circuit generally brings in AFCI protection (NEC 210.12), GFCI where the location requires it (NEC 210.8) and tamper-resistant receptacles (NEC 406.12). Many jurisdictions require a permit, and the local inspector has the final say.

Title: How To Actually Fix Short Wires In An Electrical Box (The Safe Way)
Reference: "How To Fix Short Wires In An Electrical Box" · 5,408,840 (Everyday Home Repairs, 2022-03-17) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ru4Y3W103as
Brief: The NEC requires at least 6 in. of free conductor at every box where wires are spliced or connected to a device, measured from where the conductor leaves the cable sheath, and at least 3 in. sticking out past the opening of a box smaller than 8 in. (NEC 300.14). The cable sheath must also reach at least 1/4 in. inside the box (NEC 314.17). Older homes often have short wires because every device swap trims the end. With the breaker off and the box verified dead with a tester, there are three fixes. 1) Find slack: loosen the cable clamp and gently draw cable in without nicking insulation; a service loop may give an inch or two. 2) Replace the cable where reachable from an attic, basement or crawl space; cable stapled inside the wall will not pull. 3) Pigtail: splice a short length of new wire onto each conductor (hot, neutral and ground) so a full 6 in. reaches the device; current code wording allows the spliced length to satisfy 300.14. The pigtail must match the circuit wire: same gauge (12 AWG on 20 A, 14 AWG on 15 A) and copper to copper. Aluminum branch wiring needs connectors made for it, such as the CPSC-recommended COPALUM crimp or the AlumiConn connector, and is a licensed electrician's job. Connectors must be listed for the wire: Wago 221 lever connectors take 24-12 AWG copper, stripped 11 mm and pushed fully home; wire nuts follow the maker's size chart, with no bare copper below the skirt and a tug test. Never strip extra insulation to make a wire reach, stretch a wire tight to a terminal, use push-in backstab holes to save length, or splice outside a box. Brittle, scorched or cracked insulation is a job for a licensed electrician.

Title: How to Connect a Generator to Your House the Safe, Legal Way (Interlock vs Transfer Switch)
Reference: "The BEST Way To Connect A Generator To Your House - Interlock Kit With Power Inlet Box Install" · 3,697,167 (How To Home, 2022-05-21) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fB6uI7NPxRs
Brief: A portable generator may feed house wiring only through transfer equipment that prevents the generator and the utility from supplying the panel at the same time (NEC 702.5). Three legal methods: 1) An interlock kit with a power inlet: an outdoor inlet box, whose recessed male prongs are dead until the generator runs, is wired to a two-pole breaker in the main panel, and a sliding plate on the panel cover lets the main breaker or the generator breaker be on, never both. Pros: every circuit in the panel is available. Cons: the owner manages load by switching breakers, and because NEC 702.5 requires transfer equipment to be listed, the kit must be listed for that exact panel; some inspectors accept only the panel maker's kit. 2) A manual transfer switch: a small separate panel feeding pre-selected circuits, each switched between utility and generator, so interconnection is blocked by design. 3) A meter-socket adapter between the meter and meter base, listed as a meter-mounted transfer switch and allowed only where the utility approves it. Inlets: L5-30 is 30 A at 120 V only (3,600 W, no 240 V loads); L14-30 is 30 A at 120/240 V (up to 7,200 W); 14-50 and CS6365 are 50 A at 120/240 V (up to 12,000 W). Inlet, cord and breaker all match the generator's outlet rating. With equipment that does not switch the neutral, a generator whose neutral is bonded to its frame adds a second neutral-to-ground bond, so the manual's bonded or floating status matters. CPSC: outdoors only, at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, never in a garage, with battery CO alarms inside. This is a permit job for a licensed electrician; local code may differ from the NEC and the inspector has the final say.

Title: The REAL Reason Your Plug Won't Stay In The Outlet
Reference: "Plug Won't Stay In Outlet" · 2,539,124 (Everyday Home Repairs, 2020-12-30) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0h_r2bD5bMs
Brief: A plug that won't stay in usually means the receptacle's contacts are worn out. Each slot holds a spring-formed brass contact that grips the plug blade; that grip is what keeps the plug in and what makes a tight, low-resistance electrical connection. Thousands of insertions, cords tugged at an angle and heat from high-draw loads such as vacuums, space heaters and hair dryers fatigue the metal until the contacts spread apart and no longer grip. Two-prong plugs fall out first because they have no ground pin to brace them, which is why worn outlets in hotels, kitchens and bathrooms are the familiar ones. Bent or thin plug blades, common on cheap chargers, cause the same symptom, so try the plug in another outlet first. The real problem is that the loose fit is a warning. A loose contact touches the blade over a smaller area, so resistance rises and the contact heats under load; CPSC states that loose-fitting plugs can cause overheating and fires, and that a loose connection cannot carry much current without getting hot. Heat further softens the spring metal, so the grip gets worse over time, and arcing can scorch the receptacle body. A half-pulled plug also leaves energized metal exposed to fingers. Signs: plugs that droop or drop out, a faceplate warm to the touch, brown or melted marks, crackling or buzzing, a burning smell, or power that cuts in and out when the cord moves. Spreading the plug blades is not a fix. CPSC's answer is to have the outlet replaced: breaker off, verified dead with a tester, and a new receptacle of the same rating, GFCI protected where the location now requires it and tamper-resistant where required (NEC 406.4(D)(3), 406.4(D)(5), 406.12). Scorched wires or a melted box call for a licensed electrician.

Title: Why Do LED Bulbs Glow After You Switch Them Off? (WARNING)
Brief: An LED bulb glows faintly when off because a tiny current still reaches it, from four usual sources. 1) Capacitive coupling: the switch leg to the fixture often runs beside the always-hot conductor in the same cable, and the two act as a small capacitor. With the switch open, alternating current still couples across in microamps, and long runs and three-way travelers couple more. 2) Lighted switches pass a small current through the bulb to power their indicator when off; Pass & Seymour states its illuminated switches may make LED and CFL bulbs glow or flicker when off. 3) Dimmers and smart switches wired without a neutral draw standby current through the bulb; NEC 404.2(C) requires a neutral at most new switch locations that control lighting. 4) The dangerous case: a switch wired on the neutral instead of the hot, which NEC 404.2(B) forbids; the fixture, socket and bulb base stay at 120 V when off, a shock risk when a bulb is changed. Cheap LED bulbs often use a capacitive-dropper driver feeding long strings of series LEDs, which light on microamps, while incandescents need far more current, and bulbs with switching drivers need milliamps to start. Fixes: the switch moved to the hot conductor, by an electrician; a standard switch, or an LED-rated lighted switch, in place of an old lighted one; a smart switch that uses a neutral; dimmable LEDs from the dimmer maker's compatibility list; or a load capacitor such as Lutron's LUT-MLC, made for no-neutral switches on LED and CFL loads, wired from switched hot to neutral at the fixture. Glow with buzzing or warm devices can point to a loose connection, a job for a licensed electrician. Power is off at the breaker and verified dead before work; local code may differ.

Title: 7 Outlet Wiring Mistakes I Find in Almost Every Older House
Reference: "The BIGGEST Mistakes DIYers Don't Know They Are Making When Wiring Receptacles | How To" · 12,922,797 (How To Home, 2022-08-27) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RO6Kq65HwNw
Brief: Older houses collect years of owners' receptacle work, and seven faults recur. 1) Backstabbed connections: push-in holes grip the wire with a small spring contact that can loosen as the device heats and cools, causing heat and arcing; the UL listing limits push-in terminals to 14 AWG solid copper on 15 A circuits, and side screws or screw-clamp back-wire terminals grip more firmly. 2) Reversed polarity: black (hot) belongs on the brass screws, white (neutral) on the silver screws; reversed, the outlet still works but parts of plugged-in lamps and appliances meant to be neutral become live. A plug-in tester shows it. 3) A three-prong outlet on a two-wire circuit with no ground: unless a grounding conductor is added, NEC 406.4(D)(2) allows only a two-prong replacement, a GFCI receptacle marked 'No Equipment Ground', or a three-prong outlet fed from a GFCI and marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground'. 4) Bootleg ground: a jumper from neutral to the ground screw fools a three-light tester into reading correct, but puts current-carrying neutral on appliance metal, which becomes live if the neutral opens; NEC 250.142(B) prohibits it. 5) Two wires under one screw: terminals take one conductor unless identified for more; the fix is a pigtail. 6) Poor terminations: loops wrapped counterclockwise push out as the screw tightens; manufacturers specify about three-quarters of a turn clockwise, stripped to the device's strip gauge, with no insulation under the screw or extra bare copper. 7) Aluminum branch wiring (1965 to the mid-1970s, per CPSC) on devices not marked CO/ALR; CPSC calls CO/ALR devices at best an incomplete repair and recognizes COPALUM or AlumiConn repairs at every connection, done by a licensed electrician. Power goes off at the breaker and is verified dead before any receptacle is touched; local code may differ.

Title: 10 Breaker Box Mistakes That Make a Panel Dangerous (Is Yours One?)
Reference: "10 Common Mistakes DIYers Make In Circuit Breaker Boxes" · 3,766,744 (LRN2DIY, 2023-07-29) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NF4zxBAuRoI
Brief: Most faults appear only with the dead-front off, which exposes service conductors and lugs that stay live even with the main breaker off, so opening the panel is a licensed electrician's job. 1) Double-tapped breakers: two wires under a terminal made for one; a few breakers, such as some Square D models, are labeled for two. 2) Breaker too large for the wire: copper 14 AWG is protected at 15 A, 12 AWG at 20 A, 10 AWG at 30 A (NEC 240.4(D)); the breaker protects the wire, and an upsized one lets it overheat, though air-conditioner and motor circuits follow nameplate maximums (NEC 240.4(G)). 3) Wrong-brand breakers: the panel label lists approved breakers, plus any UL Classified breakers listed for that panel; others may seat poorly on the bus and arc. 4) Neutrals and grounds together in a subpanel: they bond only at the service disconnect (NEC 250.24(A)(5)); otherwise neutral current flows on ground wires and metal. 5) Open slots and knockouts: unused breaker openings must be closed with identified filler plates (NEC 408.7), and cables enter through clamps or bushings, not bare knockout edges. 6) Several neutrals under one terminal: each neutral needs its own terminal (NEC 408.41). 7) Missing or wrong cover screws: pointed sheet-metal or drywall screws can pierce wires behind the cover, unlike the maker's blunt screws. 8) Unlabeled or vague circuit directories (NEC 408.4(A)). 9) Over-stripped or loose conductors: bare copper outside a lug, or terminals below their labeled torque, which NEC 110.14(D) requires reaching by an approved means. 10) Known problem panels: Federal Pacific Stab-Lok, linked by independent testing to breakers that fail to trip (CPSC closed its 1983 investigation without a recall), and Zinsco, whose breakers inspectors report can fuse to the aluminum bus; both are routinely flagged. Local code may differ.

Title: The Generator Mistake That Can Kill the Lineman Down the Street
Reference: "7 Backup Generator Mistakes. (Have You Made One?)" · 2,562,411 (Backyard Maine, 2024-06-14) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jNuVsFeL7vY
Brief: The mistake is backfeeding: plugging a generator into a dryer outlet, range outlet or wall receptacle with a cord that has a male plug on both ends, so the generator powers the panel backwards through that outlet's breaker. The panel connects to the utility through the meter, which measures power and disconnects nothing. If the main breaker is on, or someone switches it back on, the generator's output travels out the service drop to the pole transformer. Transformers work in both directions: the one serving a home steps distribution voltage, commonly 7,200 volts on the primary, down to 120/240 volts, so 240 volts pushed into the secondary comes out on the primary at roughly 7,200 volts (a 30-to-1 ratio). That energizes a line a repair crew may believe is dead, plus every house on the same transformer, where a neighbor can touch a downed wire. CPSC states that backfeeding through a wall outlet is an electrocution risk to utility workers and neighbors served by the same transformer, and that it bypasses some built-in household circuit protection. The cord's free end carries live, exposed prongs. The generator also tries to supply the neighborhood's connected load, which can overload it, and when utility power returns with the generator still connected, state emergency agencies warn the generator and house wiring can be severely damaged, and CPSC says backfeeding can cause electrocution or fire. The NEC requires transfer equipment that prevents interconnecting the two sources (NEC 702.5), and CPSC warned in March 2026 that male-to-male cords should never be used. The safe alternatives: cords from the generator to individual appliances, an interlock kit with an inlet, or a transfer switch installed by a licensed electrician with a permit, and the generator outdoors at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents.

Title: 9 Electrical Things Every Homeowner Wishes They'd Learned Sooner
Reference: "5 CLEVER Electrical Tricks Everyone Should Know" · 3,604,549 (LRN2DIY, 2022-04-30) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9hlo87E_GdQ
Brief: 1) The main shutoff is the main breaker in the panel, or a separate disconnect near the meter, and a legible panel directory saves time. 2) A breaker trips from an overload or a short circuit, and GFCI or AFCI breakers also from ground or arc faults; one reset is normal, repeated trips point to a fault or overload, and a breaker is never upsized, since it protects the wire (14 AWG copper at 15 A, 12 AWG at 20 A). 3) CPSC recommends testing every GFCI monthly: TEST should cut power to a plugged-in lamp and RESET restore it, and a 'dead' bathroom or garage outlet is often fed through a tripped GFCI elsewhere. 4) A non-contact voltage tester can miss voltage in armored or shielded cable, inside metal boxes or with a weak battery; it is checked on a known live outlet before and after, and silence never proves a wire is dead. 5) Warm, discolored, buzzing or burning-smelling outlets and switches, and flickering lights, point to loose connections or overloads that can arc and overheat. 6) Extension cords are temporary: NEC 400.12 bars cords as a substitute for fixed wiring, run through walls, ceilings, doorways or windows, or fastened to surfaces. 7) Wiring from 1965 to the mid-1970s may include aluminum branch circuits, which CPSC links to overheating connections; CPSC-recognized repairs (COPALUM, AlumiConn) are a licensed electrician's job. 8) A three-prong outlet doesn't prove a ground; a plug-in tester reveals open grounds and reversed polarity. 9) Good connections: wire loops go clockwise under screws, listed lever connectors accept mixed solid and stranded wire, splices stay inside boxes, and a damaged cord plug can be replaced with a listed plug wired brass-hot, silver-neutral, green-ground. Power is off at the breaker and verified dead before any work.

Title: Why Exactly Do Electric Plugs Have Holes?
Reference: "Why Do Electric Plugs Have Holes? Answered" · 8,646,225 (Silver Cymbal, 2021-02-06) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Db-dt5U3MCc
Brief: US plug-blade holes date from the earliest plugs and survive mainly for manufacturing. Harvey Hubbell's 1904 separable plug patent used flat blades set in tandem; his parallel-blade patent, filed 1912 and granted 1913, set the layout behind today's NEMA 1-15 plug. Popular accounts say some early Hubbell blades had indentations matching small bumps in the socket. Modern receptacle contacts mostly grip the blade by spring pressure and friction, and on a fully inserted plug the hole has already slid past the contacts, deeper into the receptacle, which is why plugs without holes fit just as snugly. The NEMA dimension drawing states the hole is optional and intended for manufacturing purposes only, but if used must be located where shown. In the factory, alignment rods threaded through the holes hold the blades while the plug body is molded around them, and the holes can also take shipping seals and some lockout devices. Claims that the holes save metal or date from wartime rationing don't fit: holes predate World War II by decades and the metal saved is trivial. On a polarized two-prong (NEMA 1-15) plug the wider blade is neutral, so a lamp's screw shell and a switched appliance stay on the neutral side and the switch breaks the hot. A NEMA 5-15 plug adds a round or U-shaped ground pin, longer than the blades so it connects first and disconnects last; that pin also fixes the orientation, so the blades are often both narrow. In the code, '1' means 125 V two-wire non-grounding, '5' means 125 V grounding, and '15' is the amp rating. Tamper-resistant receptacles, required in dwellings since the 2008 NEC (now 406.12), have shutters that open only when both blades push at once. A receptacle that barely grips a plug has worn contacts that can overheat.

Title: BEWARE of These 3 Common Wiring Mistakes on Outlets & Switches
Reference: "BEWARE Of These 3 Common Wiring Mistakes On Outlets & Switches" · 4,486,163 (Silver Cymbal, 2022-03-29) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=irK7l3eyB8g
Brief: 1) Wrong wire on the wrong terminal. On a receptacle, brass screws take the black (hot) wire, silver screws the white (neutral) and the green screw the bare or green ground; swapped, it still works but reverse polarity leaves the shell of a lamp socket or an appliance's internal parts live when switched off. A plug-in tester shows it. On a switch, the switch must interrupt the hot conductor, never the neutral (NEC 404.2(B)); a switch on the neutral leaves the fixture live while it is off. On a switch loop wired with two-wire cable, the white conductor used as a hot must be re-marked with tape or paint (black or red) at every termination and visible point, and may serve only as the supply to the switch, never the return (NEC 200.7(C)(1)). On three-way switches, the darker 'common' screw takes the line or the load, not a traveler. 2) The hook formed the wrong way. Terminal screws tighten clockwise, so the loop goes clockwise about three-quarters of a turn; wrapped the other way it is pushed out from under the screw. Strip length follows the gauge molded on the device (Leviton sheets give 5/8 to 3/4 inch for side wiring, by device): too much leaves bare copper that can touch the ground or the box, too little traps insulation under the screw and gives a poor, heating connection. 3) Backstabbing. Push-in holes hold the wire with a small spring contact that can loosen over time; on receptacles the UL listing limits them to 14 AWG solid copper on 15 A circuits. Screw-clamp back-wire terminals take solid or stranded wire, some two wires per terminal where the device is marked for it. Power is off at the breaker and verified dead with a tester first; local code may differ.

Title: Never Solder Wires Again - The EASY Way to Connect Them
Reference: "Never Solder Again - How to Connect Wires the EASY Way" · 4,474,145 (Silver Cymbal, 2021-03-28) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NZtwD_F7lTA
Brief: Twisting wires together and wrapping them in tape is not an acceptable splice. Solder-seal connectors (also sold as hybrid or solderless connectors) are clear heat-shrink tubes with a low-temperature solder ring in the middle and a colored adhesive ring near each end; the color marks the wire gauge range, matched to the wire size. Use: strip a short length of insulation, push the bare ends in from each side so the strands overlap under the solder ring with the insulation under the colored rings, then heat with a heat gun until the tube shrinks, the solder melts and flows into the strands, and the adhesive seals both ends; let it cool before flexing. The result is sealed against moisture, which suits automotive, trailer, marine, landscape lighting and 24-volt sprinkler wiring. Limits: most kits are sold for those uses and carry no listing for building wiring; a UL Recognized Component mark on some is for parts inside factory-built equipment, not a building-wire listing, and house wiring is mostly solid 14 and 12 AWG. The NEC requires splices made with devices identified for the use, or soldered only after the wires are already mechanically and electrically secure (NEC 110.14(B)), and connections that depend solely on solder are not permitted on grounding conductors (NEC 250.8). Solder also stiffens stranded wire, creating a break point where it flexes. Other no-solder options: crimped butt splices, color-coded by gauge (red 22-18, blue 16-14, yellow 12-10), made with a ratcheting crimper and a tug test, with heat-shrink versions for wet spots. For 120 V house wiring inside boxes, use listed twist-on wire connectors, push-in connectors, or lever connectors such as Wago 221 (UL rated 600 V, 20 A, 24-12 AWG solid or stranded), with power off at the breaker and verified dead with a tester.

Title: The #1 DIY Electrical Mistake - Can You Run Romex in Conduit?
Reference: "#1 DIY Electric Mistake - Can you use Romex Wire in Conduit?" · 2,720,570 (Silver Cymbal, 2024-03-31) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PZFJkXfThUg
Brief: NM cable (Romex is a brand name) is allowed inside conduit, and the NEC calls for it where the cable needs protection from physical damage: rigid metal conduit, IMC, EMT, Schedule 80 PVC, RTRC marked -XW or another approved means (NEC 334.15(B)), with a bushing or adapter where the cable enters and leaves the conduit. The mistake is running NM through conduit outdoors or underground, such as to a detached garage, shed, post light or outdoor receptacle. NM is not permitted in wet or damp locations (NEC 334.12(B)(4)); the inside of a raceway installed underground is a wet location (NEC 300.5(B)), and so is the inside of a raceway in a wet location above grade (NEC 300.9). Conduit does not keep water out: condensation and seepage collect inside it, and NM is not made for that. Conductors in those raceways must be listed for wet locations, such as individual THWN-2 conductors, or the run can use UF cable, which is rated for wet locations and direct burial. An attached garage is generally treated like the house, not as damp. Other problems with NM in conduit: a cable is treated as a single conductor for fill, sized by its widest dimension as a circle (Chapter 9, Note 9), and one cable may fill no more than 53 percent of the conduit (Chapter 9, Table 1), so a single flat cable can overfill 1/2-inch conduit; NM drags and jams at bends, so longer runs pull far easier as individual conductors; and stripping the sheath to pull the inner wires is not allowed, because those conductors are not marked as a standalone wire type. Several cables in one conduit need ampacity reduction for heat. Outdoor runs usually need a permit; local code may differ and the inspector has the final say.

Title: The Worst Electrical Mistake You Can Make - Backfeeding a Generator
Reference: "Worst Electrical Mistake You Can Make - Backfeeding Generators" · 2,371,256 (Silver Cymbal, 2022-02-10) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9kjpS1vfGio
Brief: Every legitimate cord follows one rule: the end that receives power has the male plug and the end that delivers power has a female connector, so live metal is always recessed. Wall receptacles are female for the same reason. A cord with a male plug on both ends, sold online as a "double male" cord and nicknamed the suicide cord, breaks that rule: once either end is plugged in, the prongs on the other end are live and exposed, and touching them means a shock or electrocution. In March 2026 CPSC told consumers to stop using male-to-male extension cords, stating they "have no legitimate household use," should never be used under any circumstances, and are typically used for backfeeding; CPSC secured removal of listings on Walmart, eBay and AliExpress from China-based sellers who did not respond to recall requests, and noted their short length puts generators close to the house, raising carbon monoxide risk. Backfeeding through one is the worst electrical mistake because it stacks several hazards at once: live exposed prongs; generator power flowing out through the meter to the pole transformer, which steps it up to distribution voltage and endangers line crews and neighbors; CPSC's warning that it bypasses some built-in household circuit protection; a main breaker that someone forgets, or switches back on; generator and house wiring damage when utility power returns; and CPSC's warning of electrocution or fire. The legal ways all keep live metal recessed and make interconnection impossible: an outdoor power inlet (its male prongs are dead until the generator is connected, the same design as an RV's shore-power inlet) with a panel interlock kit, or a manual transfer switch (NEC 702.5), installed by a licensed electrician with a permit; or plain heavy-duty outdoor cords from the generator to individual appliances.

Title: The Short-Wire Mistake Everyone Makes in the Electrical Box
Reference: "How To Fix Short Wires In An Electrical Box" · 5,408,840 (Everyday Home Repairs, 2022-03-17) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ru4Y3W103as
Brief: The mistake is connecting the new receptacle or switch straight to wires that are too short instead of adding a pigtail. With only an inch or two of wire past the box face, the conductor is pulled tight to reach the terminal, and then the device is pushed back into the box. That folding puts steady strain on the terminal: a screw connection can work loose or end up with only part of a loop under the screw head, and the wire can bend sharply right at the cable clamp. People often strip extra insulation so the wire will reach, which leaves bare copper outside the terminal close to a metal box or the ground wire, or they use the push-in backstab holes because those need only a short straight end. Push-in terminals are permitted only with 14 AWG solid copper and depend on a small spring contact. The result in every case is a weak connection, and CPSC notes that a loose connection cannot carry much current without getting hot; heat at a terminal leads to arcing, melted insulation and fire risk inside the wall, often unnoticed until the outlet is warm or dead. The NEC sets the minimum: at least 6 in. of free conductor measured from where the wire leaves the cable sheath, and 3 in. past the opening of a box smaller than 8 in. (NEC 300.14). The right fix is a pigtail: with the breaker off and the box verified dead with a tester, splice a 6 in. or longer piece of the same gauge copper wire onto each conductor using a listed lever connector or wire nut, then connect the pigtail to the device's screw or clamp terminal. Brittle insulation or aluminum wire calls for a licensed electrician.

Title: Pull THIS Out of Your Wall and Your Plugs Will Never Fall Out Again
Reference: "Plug Won't Stay In Outlet" · 2,539,124 (Everyday Home Repairs, 2020-12-30) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0h_r2bD5bMs
Brief: The fix is a new receptacle, and the choice matters. Grade: residential grade devices use lighter contacts; commercial and specification grade use heavier brass contacts and usually back-wire clamp terminals. Rating: a 15 A receptacle has two straight slots; a 20 A receptacle has a T-shaped neutral slot and needs a 20 A circuit. Tamper-resistant: the NEC requires nearly all replacements in homes to be tamper-resistant (NEC 406.4(D)(5), 406.12); shutters open only when both blades press together. Where GFCI protection is now required (bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, basements, laundry areas, near sinks), the replacement must be GFCI protected (NEC 406.4(D)(3)); where AFCI protection is now required, an AFCI receptacle (at it or upstream) or combination AFCI breaker must protect it (NEC 406.4(D)(4)); outdoors it must be weather-resistant (NEC 406.4(D)(6)). A box with no ground wire takes a non-grounding receptacle, a GFCI receptacle marked "No Equipment Ground," or a three-prong receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked "GFCI Protected" and "No Equipment Ground," never an unprotected three-prong (NEC 406.4(D)(2)). Steps: 1) turn off the breaker and verify dead with a tester; 2) note every wire and whether the brass tab between the screws is broken, which means a switched or split outlet, possibly on two breakers, so verify both halves dead, and break the tab on the new one; 3) strip in the stripper hole matching the gauge to avoid nicking copper; 4) hot to brass, neutral to silver, ground to green; loop clockwise under a screw with no insulation under the head, or insert straight into a clamp to the strip gauge; avoid push-in backstab holes; 5) tighten all screws, including unused ones; 6) fold wires in and mount (longer 6-32 screws for paneling); 7) restore power and check with a plug-in tester; press TEST and RESET on a GFCI.

Title: The Dead Outlet Mistake Everyone Makes (It's Not the Breaker)
Reference: "Is your outlet not working? See how to reset your GFCI outlets and circuit breaker" · 1,884,280 (Skobel Homes, 12y ago) · https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=trLeLJdMWWI
Brief: The common mistake with a dead outlet is checking only the panel, seeing no tripped breaker, and deciding the outlet or wiring has failed. 1) A tripped GFCI receptacle in another spot: a GFCI wired through its LOAD terminals protects every ordinary receptacle downstream on the same circuit, and those downstream outlets have no buttons of their own. The GFCI can be in a different room: one bathroom's GFCI feeding another bathroom, or a garage, basement, kitchen or laundry GFCI feeding outdoor or other outlets. Downstream outlets may carry a "GFCI Protected" sticker. A GFCI will not reset if no power reaches it, if line and load wires are reversed, or if it has reached end of life. 2) A GFCI, AFCI or dual-function breaker in the panel: a tripped handle often rests in the middle, not fully off, and can look normal; reset by pushing it fully off, then on. 3) A switched receptacle: the NEC lets a wall switch control a receptacle, or half of one, in place of a switched ceiling light in rooms other than kitchens and bathrooms, so try every nearby switch. 4) A loose connection upstream: receptacles are usually chained, and a failed push-in (backstab) or loose screw at the last working outlet or the first dead one cuts power to everything beyond it; CPSC notes a loose connection heats up under load, so this is a fire risk, not just a nuisance. How to find it: map which outlets are dead, check each with a plug-in tester, reset every GFCI in bathrooms, kitchen, garage, outdoors, basement and laundry, check the panel for mid-position handles, and try switches. Opening boxes requires the breaker off and the box verified dead with a tester; scorched or melted parts call for a licensed electrician.
